If you go to realityapologetics.com and go to the event in Dallas, which is in February, it has the information about live-streaming. What you may want to do is pay for a live-streaming based on your audience size. Okay, different sizes, there's a different schedule for different sizes. If it's an individual, if it's a family, it's a small group, if it's a church, whatever. So those details are there. But my suspicion is the whole archive is going to be available up until May. And so even though the event is in Dallas in February, you can purchase the rights to watch for your group to watch the archived copy of that event, and then just do it in situ at your school there without having to travel at all. Then you have Friday night and all day Saturday with the breaks and everything, so that you could have that student event to cap off your school year. That's the best recommendation I could make. I don't know about conferences, about other conferences for youth. I know there's a, because we attend an EV-free church in Woodruff, Wisconsin when we're up there in the summer, and they have an EV-free conference somewhere in the state somewhere, and there's about 3,000 kids that go to that. That's what I heard. But I don't know where it is and I don't know what time of year it is. So I can't help you with that. Now, as far as curriculum is concerned, we have STRU. It's not geared for high school students. It's geared for Christians. And whatever age. And the thing about the way we produce our materials, you may not, I think I'm pretty safe in saying this, that the way we produce our materials is we throw the ball so people can catch it. And if they're a high school group, they shouldn't have any trouble with understanding any of the STRU courses. And there's something like 25 or 30 of them now. We have a more recent one that just got added, the Worldview Conversation series at STRU. There are four short, simple courses, and Tim Barnett's one of the instructors, and Alan Schleiman and Robbie Lashua. So that's something. And there's all kinds of different topics. And they're broken down into sections. Watch a couple of them. There's no charge. And you can see if those, you think those would be appropriate. We have homeschoolers using those with their young people and really gaining a lot from it. Now, it may be that Sean McDowell has some curriculum that might be used. I'm just not up on this. I don't have, like, a big picture of the whole field, as it were. You could use, say, Tim Barnett's Red Pen Logic. So go to YouTube and just type in Red Pen Logic, and you'll get Tim Barnett. And these are vignettes. These are five, six, seven-minute vignettes where he takes some kind of meme or some kind of, what's that other thing they do, the little short video things, TikTok? And they're usually very critical of Christianity. And what he does is he works through it and reasons through it and red pens it like the teacher he used to be and helps not only answer the challenge, but teach you how the answer works. So those are fun, and they're very educational, and they're very accessible. I'm pretty sure there's good stuff out there that other people have produced. I just think of Sean because I know he works a lot with youth, and he's written a lot of stuff and done curriculum and stuff like that. So you may find something that he has done that you will find useful. But I think the things that we've done at Stand to Reason are adaptable. You can live stream in May to cap off the season, the whole Friday night, Saturday reality conference. You can use the STRU courses. You can cobble together a series of Red Pen Logic that Tim does, and I think that will help. Probably more out there, but that would be my suggestions. And thanks so much for your question, Carrie. Now, let's see. I've got a few more minutes here. I'm looking at scanning these. Well, this is – let's hear from Amos, all right? This is a young man of eight years down under. Do they – maybe they age faster down under than they do here. Oh, Austrian. Oh, okay. Oh, yeah, you're right, Austrian. Okay, well, let's hear from Amos. Hello, Mr. Craig. My name is Amos.

Amen, and I am eight years old. I live in Vienna, Austria, and my question is, why we have to pray in front of the abortion clinic and not at home? All right, Mr. Amos, I appreciate your call. Dankeschön. And you have a point. It isn't as if one's prayers themselves, I think, are going to be more effective regarding an abortion clinic if you're at the abortion clinic itself as opposed to being at home. Wherever you pray for those things, God is equally available to you to answer the prayer, to respond to the prayer, okay? However, I think there is another factor, and it isn't God listening to your prayer itself. When you're at an abortion clinic and you're praying, something else is happening too. You are there where abortions are taking place. And I'll just say this, it feels different. It's one thing to pray in your room or in your home with your family about the abortion clinic, and God is fine with that. But when you're there at the place, and you know what's going on on the other side of those doors, you can pray exactly the same prayer, but it's going to feel different to you. I guarantee it. It's going to be more real to you. You are going to pray with more intensity. You are going to pray with more feeling. And I think that sometimes that makes a difference with God. The intensity that we pray with, the feeling that we pray with, the focus that we have when we pray, I'm tempted to think that makes a difference with God. Now, I'm not an expert at prayer by no means. And I have a hard time myself figuring out how prayer works and how some prayers seem to be more effective than others. But it just seems to me, if you're praying in kind of a lukewarm way, in America we say lackadaisical, like a ho-hum, ho-hum. Okay, God, we pray for this, that, and the other. It isn't that that's not a good prayer, but it may not be the best prayer. If you're right there where these things are happening, and you're calling out to God to do something in the lives of those women to keep their children from dying, that is, I guarantee you, going to feel more real, and then you're going to pray with more intensity, with more strength, with more vigor. And I have a suspicion that's going to make the prayers better prayers, more effective prayers. Not sure, but I think so. So that's one factor that is different when you're praying at the location of something. And by the way, this could be true. Look, you could be praying for somebody's wedding or marriage. They're getting married, right? You're going to pray for their marriage. Well, you can pray at home, but if you're at the ceremony and you pray for them while it's happening, can you see how that's going to feel more real, and you're probably going to pray more vigorously or with more energy or more conviction? I think so. There's something else that's going on, though. And that is, when you are praying in front of an abortion clinic, you are visible to other people. You are physically present. It's like you are making a personal statement. And if there are a lot of people there that are praying, again, it just seems to me it's going to have a greater effect. So what is the prayer for? When you're praying, you are praying at an abortion clinic where children are being killed before they're born. That's what an abortion is. You are praying, presumably, that that wouldn't happen or that women that go to that clinic to get an abortion will change their minds. Now, it seems to me if a woman is going to an abortion clinic to have an abortion and the only people she sees or talks to are the people who want to give her the abortion, sell her the abortion, she is more likely to go through with it than if she has to see, even if the Christians who are praying are not obstructing anything, they're not getting in the way, she's still going to see them. And she's aware that there are people that are appealing to God on behalf of her and her baby. And I think that show of strength, that show of prayer, display of prayer strength by the people has an effect on the way people think about this issue. Now, some people might get mad at it. I get that. And I know that in England, it's against the law to pray in front of an abortion clinic, even if you're praying silently. Or at least some places in England, I've seen videotapes where people get arrested. What are you doing? I'm praying. You can't do that here. I'm praying silently. That's illegal. You're under arrest. That happens, right? But part of it, I think they're afraid of the way it looks and the influence it might have on people when they come to get an abortion and they realize there's some person there or multiple people that are praying right now for them and their children. So that's something that's going to happen when you're at the abortion clinic and it's not going to happen when you're just at home praying. I'm not saying that the prayer can't be effective at home. I'm saying when you're at a clinic and you're in the actual location, and this applies to a lot of different things, it does something to the way you pray, makes your prayers more, in a sense, energetic, powerful, effective, I think, maybe. And it is a witness to other people, to people who don't want you to be there and there you're standing in defense of the unborn, and to mothers who are thinking about getting an abortion and maybe just the presence there, they see people praying, will be enough to change their mind. So there you have it. Very glad to hear from you, Amos. Nicely done, young man. Give me a call anytime you want to chat. All right, that's it for today. Greg Koukl for Stand to Reason. Give them heaven, friends. Bye-bye now.
